quotes.text: The sloppiness of Scott Walker's new album is built into its title. Bish Bosch is bish bosh — a thankless task done in a slapdash way.

But what's really amazing about Bish Bosch is that all of its myriad components are somehow pulled in to exist on the same insane planet. The source of the gravity? Walker's immense, disgruntled-god croon, of course. Much like the works of Hieronymus Bosch—the album's namesake painter—it's foolish to try to absorb the whole piece on first listen, but isolated portions are readily appreciable in their own right.

The instrumentation might seem relatively sensible – the closest you'll find to butchery here is the incessant menacing scrape of machetes in Tar – but Walker's tenor in a wind-tunnel croon is still the loneliest sound imaginable, and the lyrics are just as obtuse yet death and decay-driven as ever.
Building upon his groundbreaking last two albums, Bish Bosch is Scott Walker's (aka Noel Scott Engel) latest aural descent into the abyss.

Scott Walker albums are like reading James Joyce's Ulysses. It's impossible to digest in only one sitting and can even drive you mad with its labyrinthine web of allusions during a second, fifth, or tenth pass. Over 45 years into his recording career, the former U.K. boy band semi-star (as one of The Walker Brothers) is still crafting art pieces that are as harrowing as they are visionary.

Scott Walker might be little more than a month shy of his 70th birthday, and a grandpa to boot, but no one in any age group has come anywhere near his reckless musical daring – at least no one from the pop or rock milieu.

His work since Climate of Hunter (1984) – especially the trilogy that began with Tilt (1995) and continued with The Drift (2006) and now Bish Bosch – has profoundly alienated many fans of the beautifully-orchestrated albums that once showcased his (still) magnificent baritone.

But it's quite another matter to approach the compositions of a `60s pop star who turned his back so radically and irreversibly on the mainstream that his albums over the past three decades have pretty much dispensed entirely with melody and conventional song structure to substitute horrifying soundscapes and nightmarish, surrealist imagery.

If blink-and-miss flourishes of strings or brass here recall, let's say, Plastic Palace People, the flash of recognition is allowed to last only a few seconds before Walker squashes it with a discordant surf-guitar assault (Tar), a bit of flatulence (quite literally, in Corps de Blah) or colossal jackhammer drums. Orchestration is not melodic adornment here, but more the sound of fear.

The way Walker uses protracted stretches of silence in the disc's 22-minute centerpiece, SDSS 1416+13B (Zercon, a Flagpole sitter), is particularly exciting, making the listener apprehensive about what variety of sonic hell is about to be unleashed.

The sharpening of machetes as percussion in Tar go right through you. The words of Pilgrim double as the song's percussion. And the sleigh bells in The Day the "Conducator" Died (An XMas Song) make Walker singing a self-help checklist all the creepier.
